title: KX Gives Back: How a local nonprofit is helping people heal from their trauma - NewsBreak
text: MINOT, ND ( KXNET ) — A local nonprofit is assisting those who have suffered trauma through a holistic approach. In this month’s KX Gives Back, reporter Megan Topping got to know some of the people who run it. Trauma is an emotional response to a distressing event that can overwhelm a person’s ability to cope. The long-term effects can include sleeping disorders, flashbacks, extreme tension, anxiety, depression, and addictions. Shelly Bohl, the executive director of the business, called The Difference – A Holistic Approach, said many people suffer from past traumas, and they often believe there is nothing that can be done when in fact, there is help available. “I had been interested in and learning about holistic healing for many, many, many years and when I worked at Domestic Violence I recognized that even though these victims were strong enough to leave their abuse, the trauma they had experienced was going to stay with them the rest of their life,” Bohl said, “and until it had been released, it would affect every aspect of their life and so when I retired I developed this non-profit so that we could provide this healing to all victims of trauma in North-Central North Dakota.” The Difference – A Holistic Approach uses energy healing, a holistic practice that activates the body’s subtle energy systems to remove the blocks that have been created from trauma. By doing this, Bohl says there are many benefits, such as stress release and relaxation, which triggers the body’s natural healing abilities. Bohl said energy healing isn’t about forcing anything; it’s about the releasing of energy blocks so natural healing can take place. “We are meant to have a good quality of life, a peaceful, a joyful life is my belief, and anything that keeps us from having that quality of life is not for us to hold onto,” Bohl said. “So my goal is to bring a better quality of life so that the people I meet on the street have that glow about them so they have that peace so they can be smiling and enjoy the life that they are meant to lead.” There are 19 practitioners who work with the nonprofit. Bohl said making an appointment is a simple process, and the only qualification is having some form of trauma. “So how it works, if you’re interested, come in and fill out a simple intake form, that way I can get the statistics that I need to write grants to provide funding for this work, give you the list of practitioners, you make an appointment, you go for a session and they would send me the bill,” she said. “Once I pay that bill I send you an evaluation to see if it helped or how it may have helped and we will pay for a total of three sessions. You can go to the same one three times, you can go to three different ones, and the results we’re getting on these evaluations are amazing. They are showing that we truly are making a difference.” Dena Filler, the president of the nonprofit, spent 29 years working with the Domestic Violence Crisis Center in Minot. She says her background in working with trauma made her want to help people even more with these practices. “Being with Shelly and meeting some of the individuals that we’ve helped has made a difference in my life,” Filler said. “Also because I have been able to use that holistic healing on myself and on my family so that I know these services are available and I think that’s just important.” Bohl says the goal of the sessions isn’t to completely heal you right away; it is to show people what is possible, what is available, and how it can help you on your journey to healing. As part of our KX Gives Back initiative, we brought lunch and got to catch up with the people who lead the nonprofit. The Difference – A Holistic Approach is strictly funded by grant dollars, charitable donations, and fundraisers. Through the nonprofit, they told us they were able to help a veteran with PTSD. The veteran was so amazed by how much better he felt and by the help he received that he decided to start a fundraiser for them. On October 1, he says he’s driving from Alaska to Argentina to raise awareness and funds for the nonprofit.
